screens.title: Implementing Advanced Logging with journald and rsyslog
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on building a resilient logging pipeline using journald as a local collector and rsyslog as a flexible forwarder. You will learn how to make journald persistent, cap its disk usage, and forward selected messages for centralized storage. We will also cover advanced journalctl filters and output formats you can use to find precise events quickly during incident response. Then we move to rsyslog: how rules are written, how to route cron or mail messages to dedicated files, and how to secure remote forwarding with TLS. Throughout, I will show concrete configuration snippets and explain common mistakes to avoid, such as broad rules that capture messages before specific ones or certificate path errors that silently block forwarding. By the end of this lesson you will understand how these components complement each other: journald gives structured local logs; rsyslog scales, routes, and encrypts; together they help preserve log integrity. Think of this chapter as the operational playbook you need to keep logs persistent, searchable, and safe from tampering.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Implementing Advanced Logging

Make logs persist across reboots, query them precisely, route them with rules, and protect them in transit.

Start by configuring journald to store logs on disk and limit usage. Use journalctl to slice time ranges, priorities, and service fields. Then build rsyslog rules to split messages into files, stop broad processing with & stop, and forward sensitive logs to a remote server over TLS.

In this lesson

What you will practice

  • Enable persistent journald storage and set SystemMaxUse/SystemKeepFree.
  • Use journalctl filters and JSON output for automation.
  • Create rsyslog rules for cron logs and secure auth logs with TLS.
Coming up
journald
journalctl
rsyslog
Visual concept
journald
Structured, local collector
rsyslog
Routing and secure forwarding
Lines indicate forward or write destinations. Use journald for local persistence and rsyslog for long-term aggregation and TLS-protected transport.
Explore Key Topics
Persistence: Storage=persistent creates /var/log/journal so logs survive reboot and can be limited.
Filtering: Use journalctl --since/--until and -p for precise searches and -o json for automation.
TLS Forwarding: Configure omfwd or omfwd-style actions with gtls to protect authpriv messages in transit.

Third, you'll create rsyslog rules to filter, route, and stop processing of messages, including sending cron logs to a dedicated file. Fourth, you'll implement secure remote logging by configuring rsyslog to use TLS with appropriate CA and certificate settings. Each objective includes a short rationale: persistence protects data across reboots, filtering speeds incident response, precise rules prevent log duplication, and TLS preserves confidentiality and integrity. Throughout, we emphasize verification and troubleshooting steps so you can confirm configurations and recover from common issues. These skills directly reduce mean time to detection and secure your audit trail.

screens.title: Skills and Troubleshooting Goals
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond configuration, this chapter ensures you can verify and recover logging systems. You will check service health with systemctl, inspect journald and rsyslog logs for errors, and validate configuration syntax before restart. Practical checks include verifying /var/log/journal exists after enabling persistence, using ls -ld to inspect permissions, and confirming rsyslog can write to target paths. You will learn to identify common failure modes: permission problems that block writes, full disks that stop logging, firewall rules that block remote ports, and certificate path mismatches that break TLS. For integrity, you will use tamper-detection tools and forward logs to a dedicated remote server so attackers cannot easily alter local files. Each skill pairs with a verification step: restart the service, then use journalctl -u to watch for immediate errors, and tail target log files to confirm messages arrive. These checks make logging robust and auditable in production environments.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Verification

Verify and Troubleshoot Logging

Checks and quick commands to confirm journald and rsyslog are healthy.

Service & Permission Checks
  • Use systemctl status systemd-journald and systemctl status rsyslog to see immediate service errors.
  • Confirm /var/log/journal exists and has correct ownership for journald to write persistent logs.
  • Tail unit logs with journalctl -u rsyslog to spot parsing or TLS errors after restart.
Disk, Firewall & Certificates
  • Check df -h to avoid disk exhaustion; SystemMaxUse and SystemKeepFree prevent journald from filling disks.
  • Ensure ports 514 or 6514 are open for rsyslog traffic and not blocked by a firewall.
  • Validate certificate chains and file permissions for TLS; mismatched paths cause silent failures.
Integrity & Recovery

Forward logs to a dedicated remote server and use file integrity tools to detect tampering. If journald or rsyslog fail, revert recent changes and restart services in a controlled window.

Quick Command Cheatsheet
sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald
ls -ld /var/log/journal
journalctl -u rsyslog -f
sudo systemctl restart rsyslog
# tail target log files to confirm delivery

screens.title: What is journald and why persistence matters
screens.narratorSegment: journald is the structured logging component of systemd that collects messages from the kernel, systemd services, and applications that write to standard output or standard error. By default many distributions configure it to store logs in volatile memory, which means logs are lost across reboots. That behavior is acceptable for ephemeral systems, but for production and audit needs you must preserve logs across restarts. Enabling persistent storage by setting Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald. conf creates the directory /var/log/journal and writes binary, indexed log files to disk. You also need to consider disk usage: SystemMaxUse caps total journal consumption, while SystemKeepFree guarantees a minimum amount of free space remains. A practical example: set Storage=persistent, SystemMaxUse=500M and SystemKeepFree=1G for a small server to avoid filling the partition. A common misconception is to rely only on journal rotation; without SystemKeepFree you can still starve the filesystem. Always verify that /var/log/journal exists, check permissions so systemd-journald can write, and restart systemd-journald to apply changes. The core takeaway: persistent journald preserves forensic evidence and improves post-incident analysis, but you must set sensible limits to avoid operational impact.

content.html:
Chapter 1.4 › journald Persistence
Definition

journald: systemd's structured journal

A binary, indexed log store collecting kernel, service, and application messages. It supports structured fields for precise filtering.

Why persistence matters: keeps logs across reboots for audits and postmortems.
Limits: SystemMaxUse prevents logs from filling disk; SystemKeepFree reserves free space for system operations.
Misconception: Enabling persistence without limits can still cause disk exhaustion.
Example configuration
# /etc/systemd/journald.conf
Storage=persistent
SystemMaxUse=500M
SystemKeepFree=1G
Checklist & Example Commands
  • Enable persistence: edit journald.conf and set Storage=persistent.
  • Restart service: sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald and confirm /var/log/journal exists: ls -ld /var/log/journal
  • Check current usage: journalctl --disk-usage
Key Takeaway

Persistent journald plus sensible size limits balance forensic needs and safe disk consumption.

screens.title: journalctl: advanced filtering and outputs
screens.narratorSegment: journalctl is the query engine for the systemd journal; learning advanced filters turns vast logs into precise answers. You can combine time ranges with --since and --until, restrict by unit with -u, and filter by priority using -p followed by a level like err or warning. System fields let you target process identifiers or executable names using selectors such as _PID=1234 or _COMM=sshd. For example, to see error messages from sshd on a particular day use journalctl -u sshd --since "2023-01-01" --until "2023-01-02" -p err. Output modes change how you consume results: -o json is handy when you need to pipe entries into parsers or external tools, -o verbose shows all journal metadata, and -f streams live messages for monitoring. For audit use, journalctl _AUDIT_LOGIN=yes surfaces login attempts recorded by the audit subsystem. A common misconception is that journalctl -u alone is always sufficient; in complex incidents you often need to combine -u with priority, time windows, or field selectors to isolate the root cause. Practice: run example queries, then pipe -o json into jq or your script for automation. The skill is both query fluency and knowing which output to use for the next step.

content.html:
Chapter 1.4 › journalctl Filters
Commands & Outputs

Filter by time, unit, priority, or field

journalctl -u sshd --since "2023-01-01" --until "2023-01-02" -p err
journalctl -k -p warning --since "2 hours ago"
journalctl _PID=1234
journalctl _COMM=nginx -p crit -o json

Use -o json to feed logs to parsers. Use -f to follow live output during incident triage. Use field selectors for exact process or binary matches.

Practical example and automation

If you need authentication errors from the last hour in JSON for a scripted alert, use a time window with priority and JSON output, then pipe to your tool.

journalctl -u sshd --since "1 hour ago" -p err -o json | jq '.MESSAGE'
Key Takeaway

Use combined filters and structured output to reduce noise and enable tool integration during response.

screens.title: Forwarding from journald to rsyslog
screens.narratorSegment: journald and rsyslog often operate together: journald collects and stores structured entries locally, while rsyslog can receive those messages for processing, routing, and forwarding. journald supports forwarding to syslog by toggling options in journald. conf such as ForwardToSyslog=yes and ForwardToKMsg or ForwardToConsole when needed. In practice you enable ForwardToSyslog=yes so journald delivers a copy of messages to the system syslog socket, where rsyslog listens. rsyslog then applies its rule engine: selectors, actions, and optional stops. A typical flow is journald collects a message, it writes to /var/log/journal and forwards a copy to rsyslog which evaluates rules, writes to files, and forwards remote logs. A practical example: enable forwarding in journald, then add a rsyslog rule to capture authpriv.* and forward it. A misconception is thinking forwarding disables journald storage; forwarding is additive—both can store the same message. When designing pipelines, decide which system is authoritative for long-term retention and configure rotation or external aggregation accordingly. The key is using journald for structured capture and rsyslog for flexible delivery. Forwarding from journald to rsyslog means journald collects and can forward; rsyslog receives forwarded messages to filter, route, and securely forward to remote stores.. In practical terms, how journald and rsyslog work together for local collection and remote aggregation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Chapter 1.4 › journald → rsyslog
Process Flow

Local capture then flexible processing

Step 1: journald receives kernel and service messages.
Step 2: Enable ForwardToSyslog=yes so journald sends copies to syslog socket.
Step 3: rsyslog reads socket, applies rules, writes to files, or forwards remotely.
Remember: forwarding is additive. journald can retain local binary logs while rsyslog handles distribution and long-term aggregation.
Concrete example
# /etc/systemd/journald.conf
ForwardToSyslog=yes
# restart journald after change
sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald

# rsyslog will now receive messages from journald via the syslog socket
Key Takeaway

Use journald for reliable local collection and rsyslog for policy-based routing and remote aggregation.

screens.title: rsyslog basics: selectors, actions, and & stop
screens.narratorSegment: rsyslog uses a rule engine composed of selectors and actions to decide what to do with each message. A selector is a facility and priority pair like authpriv.* or cron. info that matches a class of messages. An action tells rsyslog where to send matching messages: a file path, a remote target, or a program to execute. Rules are processed in order, top to bottom. This ordering is important: a broad rule early in the sequence can capture messages before a more specific rule runs. To avoid that, you can append & stop after an action to prevent further processing of the same message. For example, mail.* /var/log/mail. log followed by & stop ensures mail messages are written to /var/log/mail. log and not to /var/log/messages. A common misconception is that duplicate writes are harmless; in practice duplicates can inflate storage and complicate analysis. A practical example: create /etc/rsyslog. d/10-mail-logs. conf with mail.* /var/log/mail. log and & stop, then restart rsyslog. Always test by generating a message and confirming it appears only in the intended file. Proper rule ordering and use of & stop make routing precise and efficient.

keyIdea.title: Rule engine
keyIdea.text: Use facility.priority selectors and actions. Add & stop to prevent further processing and avoid duplicates.

content.html:
Chapter 1.4 › rsyslog Rules
Core Concept

Selectors and actions

A selector identifies messages by facility and priority. An action writes or forwards matching messages. Rules are sequential.

Example rule file
# /etc/rsyslog.d/10-mail-logs.conf
mail.*                                      /var/log/mail.log
& stop
Why ordering matters
  • Rules run in order; a broad rule early can capture messages meant for a specific rule later.
  • Use & stop to ensure the message isn't processed by later rules that might duplicate it.
  • Test by sending a test message and observing target files to confirm single delivery.
Common Mistake

Placing a catch-all rule before specific rules causes messages to be handled incorrectly; always place specific rules first or use & stop.

screens.title: Hands-on: Filtering cron messages to a dedicated file
screens.narratorSegment: This practical walkthrough shows how to route all cron messages of info priority or higher to a dedicated log file and then stop further processing. First, create /etc/rsyslog. d/20-cron-info. conf as root with the content cron. info /var/log/cron_info. log followed by & stop. This selector matches the cron facility at info and higher. After saving, restart rsyslog and generate a cron log so you can observe the effect. You can add a temporary crontab entry that runs logger with a short message once per minute, or manually use logger to simulate a cron entry. Then use tail -f /var/log/cron_info. log to watch messages arrive. A common misconception is that rsyslog will automatically create directories with proper permissions; ensure /var/log/cron_info. log is writable by rsyslog or that rsyslog can create it with correct ownership. If messages still land in /var/log/messages, check rule ordering and ensure & stop is present. This exercise reinforces how a small rule isolates a facility into its own file and prevents duplication, making it easier to monitor cron behavior in production. Hands-on: Filtering cron messages to a dedicated file means add cron.info /var/log/cron_info.log and & stop, restart rsyslog, then generate a test cron message and confirm it appears only in cron_info.log.. In practical terms, create an rsyslog rule and verify delivery with a test cron entry. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Chapter 1.4 › rsyslog: cron routing
Code Walkthrough

Create the rule

sudo tee /etc/rsyslog.d/20-cron-info.conf > /dev/null <<EOF
# Route cron messages of 'info' priority and higher to a dedicated file
cron.info                       /var/log/cron_info.log
& stop # Stop processing this message after writing to cron_info.log
EOF
sudo systemctl restart rsyslog
After restarting, generate a test message with logger or a temporary crontab entry and check /var/log/cron_info.log with tail -f to confirm arrival.
Simulation steps
  1. Create rule file and restart rsyslog.
  2. Simulate a cron message: sudo logger -p cron.info "Test cron message from Cohortia".
  3. Confirm: tail -f /var/log/cron_info.log
Key Takeaway

Small, focused rules with & stop let you separate and monitor specific facilities without affecting global logs.

screens.title: Secure remote logging with rsyslog over TLS
screens.narratorSegment: Secure remote logging is essential to prevent interception or tampering of sensitive log streams. rsyslog supports TLS by using a gtls netstream driver. On the client, you configure global default netstream driver settings including DefaultNetstreamDriver="gtls" and DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile pointing to your CA certificate so the client can verify the server. Optionally, you can configure DefaultNetstreamDriverCertFile and DefaultNetstreamDriverKeyFile for mutual authentication. Then you create an action that uses omfwd to forward messages to a remote IP and port using TCP with TLS enabled—by using StreamDriverMode="1" and StreamDriverAuthMode="anon" or x509/certvalid depending on whether client certs are required. An example action forwards authpriv.* to a remote server on port 6514. On the server side, imtcp with TLS options and proper certificate files must be configured to receive connections. A common pitfall is incorrect file paths or permissions on certificates, which silently prevent TLS handshakes. Test TLS by generating an auth message and verifying it arrives on the server; check journalctl -u rsyslog for TLS errors if it does not. The key is matching driver, CA, and certificate settings on both ends. Secure remote logging with rsyslog over TLS means set defaultnetstreamdriver to gtls, reference ca and cert files, and use omfwd with streamdrivermode to require tls for remote forwarding.. In practical terms, configure client-side tls and global driver settings for encrypted forwarding. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Chapter 1.4 › rsyslog TLS
Client Configuration
Define global TLS driver settings and forward authpriv messages to the remote server over TCP with TLS.
# /etc/rsyslog.d/60-secure-auth.conf
module(load="omfwd") # Output module for forwarding

global(
    DefaultNetstreamDriver="gtls"
    DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile="/etc/rsyslog.certs/ca.pem"
    # DefaultNetstreamDriverCertFile and KeyFile if client certs are used
)

authpriv.* action(type="omfwd"
                  Target="REMOTE_LOG_SERVER_IP"
                  Port="6514"
                  Protocol="tcp"
                  StreamDriverMode="1"
                  StreamDriverAuthMode="anon")
Server considerations & testing
  • Server must load imtcp with TLS configured and present a certificate signed by the CA the client trusts.
  • Ensure certificate files are readable by rsyslog and have correct permissions to allow TLS handshakes.
  • Test by generating auth logs and verifying they arrive or by inspecting rsyslog unit logs for TLS errors.
Key Takeaway

TLS requires matching driver and certificate configuration on both ends; verify paths and permissions and check unit logs for handshake errors.

screens.title: journalctl output modes and when to use them
screens.narratorSegment: journalctl supports multiple output formats and choosing the right one depends on your goal. Use the default pager output for human reading and troubleshooting at the console; it formats messages in a readable timeline. Placing certificates in a world-readable path or leaving wrong permissions causes handshake failures or key disclosure risks.

screens.title: Common logging issues and how to resolve them
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting logging systems requires a structured approach because similar symptoms can have different causes. Start by checking service status with systemctl status rsyslog or systemctl status systemd-journald to see immediate failure messages. Check journalctl -u for unit-specific logs. Permissions issues are frequent: if rsyslog cannot write to a target file, verify ownership and mode. Disk space exhaustion is another common cause; use df -h and examine journald settings—SystemMaxUse and SystemKeepFree—to remedy runaway journal growth. Rule order errors appear when a broad selector earlier captures messages that specific rules should handle; use & stop to prevent duplicates and reorder files so specific rules load first. For remote logging, ensure firewalls allow the chosen ports (UDP/TCP 514 or TLS 6514) and that certificate paths and chains are correct; mismatched or unreadable cert files will block TLS. Finally, check for silent failures by tailing logs and using test messages with logger to trace delivery. The key idea is methodical checks: service health, file permissions, disk, rule logic, network, and certificates. This checklist reduces guesswork when logs stop being delivered or are missing. Chapter 1.4 › Lab Walkthrough
Part 1: journald persistence
sudo sed -i 's/^#Storage=.*/Storage=persistent/' /etc/systemd/journald.conf
sudo sed -i 's/^#SystemMaxUse=.*/SystemMaxUse=500M/' /etc/systemd/journald.conf
sudo sed -i 's/^#SystemKeepFree=.*/SystemKeepFree=1G/' /etc/systemd/journald.conf
sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald
ls -ld /var/log/journal

Confirm the directory exists and that journald writes to it after the restart.

Part 2: cron rule
sudo tee /etc/rsyslog.d/20-cron-info.conf > /dev/null <<EOF
cron.info                       /var/log/cron_info.log
& stop
EOF
sudo systemctl restart rsyslog
# Test
sudo logger -p cron.info "Test cron message from Cohortia"
tail -f /var/log/cron_info.log

Adjust file ownership if rsyslog cannot write to the target file.

Part 3: TLS forwarding (client-side)
sudo mkdir -p /etc/rsyslog.certs
sudo tee /etc/rsyslog.certs/ca.pem > /dev/null <<EOF
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
# Placeholder CA content for lab
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
EOF
sudo tee /etc/rsyslog.d/60-secure-auth.conf > /dev/null <<EOF
module(load="omfwd")

global(
    DefaultNetstreamDriver="gtls"
    DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile="/etc/rsyslog.certs/ca.pem"
)

authpriv.* action(type="omfwd" Target="REMOTE_LOG_SERVER_IP" Port="6514" Protocol="tcp" StreamDriverMode="1" StreamDriverAuthMode="anon")
EOF
sudo systemctl restart rsyslog
sudo logger -p authpriv.info "Test secure auth log from Cohortia"
# Check journalctl -u rsyslog for TLS errors
Replace REMOTE_LOG_SERVER_IP with your test server. On failure, inspect rsyslog logs and certificate permissions.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on building a resilient logging pipeline using journald as a local collector and rsyslog as a flexible forwarder. You will learn how to make journald persistent, cap its disk usage, and forward selected messages for centralized storage. We will also cover advanced journalctl filters and output formats you can use to find precise events quickly during incident response. Then we move to rsyslog: how rules are written, how to route cron or mail messages to dedicated files, and how to secure remote forwarding with TLS. Throughout, I will show concrete configuration snippets and explain common mistakes to avoid, such as broad rules that capture messages before specific ones or certificate path errors that silently block forwarding. By the end of this lesson you will understand how these components complement each other: journald gives structured local logs; rsyslog scales, routes, and encrypts; together they help preserve log integrity. Think of this chapter as the operational playbook you need to keep logs persistent, searchable, and safe from tampering.

These objectives guide the practical skills you'll master. First, you'll configure journald for persistent storage, set limits such as SystemMaxUse and SystemKeepFree, and enable forwarding so logs can be consumed by rsyslog. Second, you'll learn advanced journalctl filters and output options so you can slice logs by time range, priority, process, or field, and export JSON for automation. Third, you'll create rsyslog rules to filter, route, and stop processing of messages, including sending cron logs to a dedicated file. Fourth, you'll implement secure remote logging by configuring rsyslog to use TLS with appropriate CA and certificate settings. Each objective includes a short rationale: persistence protects data across reboots, filtering speeds incident response, precise rules prevent log duplication, and TLS preserves confidentiality and integrity. Throughout, we emphasize verification and troubleshooting steps so you can confirm configurations and recover from common issues. These skills directly reduce mean time to detection and secure your audit trail.

Beyond configuration, this chapter ensures you can verify and recover logging systems. You will check service health with systemctl, inspect journald and rsyslog logs for errors, and validate configuration syntax before restart. Practical checks include verifying /var/log/journal exists after enabling persistence, using ls -ld to inspect permissions, and confirming rsyslog can write to target paths. You will learn to identify common failure modes: permission problems that block writes, full disks that stop logging, firewall rules that block remote ports, and certificate path mismatches that break TLS. For integrity, you will use tamper-detection tools and forward logs to a dedicated remote server so attackers cannot easily alter local files. Each skill pairs with a verification step: restart the service, then use journalctl -u to watch for immediate errors, and tail target log files to confirm messages arrive. These checks make logging robust and auditable in production environments.

journald is the structured logging component of systemd that collects messages from the kernel, systemd services, and applications that write to standard output or standard error. By default many distributions configure it to store logs in volatile memory, which means logs are lost across reboots. That behavior is acceptable for ephemeral systems, but for production and audit needs you must preserve logs across restarts. Enabling persistent storage by setting Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald. conf creates the directory /var/log/journal and writes binary, indexed log files to disk. You also need to consider disk usage: SystemMaxUse caps total journal consumption, while SystemKeepFree guarantees a minimum amount of free space remains. A practical example: set Storage=persistent, SystemMaxUse=500M and SystemKeepFree=1G for a small server to avoid filling the partition. A common misconception is to rely only on journal rotation; without SystemKeepFree you can still starve the filesystem. Always verify that /var/log/journal exists, check permissions so systemd-journald can write, and restart systemd-journald to apply changes. The core takeaway: persistent journald preserves forensic evidence and improves post-incident analysis, but you must set sensible limits to avoid operational impact.

journalctl is the query engine for the systemd journal; learning advanced filters turns vast logs into precise answers. You can combine time ranges with --since and --until, restrict by unit with -u, and filter by priority using -p followed by a level like err or warning. System fields let you target process identifiers or executable names using selectors such as _PID=1234 or _COMM=sshd. For example, to see error messages from sshd on a particular day use journalctl -u sshd --since "2023-01-01" --until "2023-01-02" -p err. Output modes change how you consume results: -o json is handy when you need to pipe entries into parsers or external tools, -o verbose shows all journal metadata, and -f streams live messages for monitoring. For audit use, journalctl _AUDIT_LOGIN=yes surfaces login attempts recorded by the audit subsystem. A common misconception is that journalctl -u alone is always sufficient; in complex incidents you often need to combine -u with priority, time windows, or field selectors to isolate the root cause. Practice: run example queries, then pipe -o json into jq or your script for automation. The skill is both query fluency and knowing which output to use for the next step.

journald and rsyslog often operate together: journald collects and stores structured entries locally, while rsyslog can receive those messages for processing, routing, and forwarding. journald supports forwarding to syslog by toggling options in journald. conf such as ForwardToSyslog=yes and ForwardToKMsg or ForwardToConsole when needed. In practice you enable ForwardToSyslog=yes so journald delivers a copy of messages to the system syslog socket, where rsyslog listens. rsyslog then applies its rule engine: selectors, actions, and optional stops. A typical flow is journald collects a message, it writes to /var/log/journal and forwards a copy to rsyslog which evaluates rules, writes to files, and forwards remote logs. A practical example: enable forwarding in journald, then add a rsyslog rule to capture authpriv.* and forward it. A misconception is thinking forwarding disables journald storage; forwarding is additive—both can store the same message. rsyslog uses a rule engine composed of selectors and actions to decide what to do with each message. A selector is a facility and priority pair like authpriv.* or cron. info that matches a class of messages. An action tells rsyslog where to send matching messages: a file path, a remote target, or a program to execute. Rules are processed in order, top to bottom. This ordering is important: a broad rule early in the sequence can capture messages before a more specific rule runs. To avoid that, you can append & stop after an action to prevent further processing of the same message. For example, mail.* /var/log/mail. log followed by & stop ensures mail messages are written to /var/log/mail. log and not to /var/log/messages. A common misconception is that duplicate writes are harmless; in practice duplicates can inflate storage and complicate analysis. A practical example: create /etc/rsyslog. d/10-mail-logs. conf with mail.* /var/log/mail. log and & stop, then restart rsyslog. Always test by generating a message and confirming it appears only in the intended file. Proper rule ordering and use of & stop make routing precise and efficient.

Secure remote logging is essential to prevent interception or tampering of sensitive log streams. rsyslog supports TLS by using a gtls netstream driver. On the client, you configure global default netstream driver settings including DefaultNetstreamDriver="gtls" and DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile pointing to your CA certificate so the client can verify the server. Optionally, you can configure DefaultNetstreamDriverCertFile and DefaultNetstreamDriverKeyFile for mutual authentication. Then you create an action that uses omfwd to forward messages to a remote IP and port using TCP with TLS enabled—by using StreamDriverMode="1" and StreamDriverAuthMode="anon" or x509/certvalid depending on whether client certs are required. An example action forwards authpriv.* to a remote server on port 6514. On the server side, imtcp with TLS options and proper certificate files must be configured to receive connections. A common pitfall is incorrect file paths or permissions on certificates, which silently prevent TLS handshakes. Test TLS by generating an auth message and verifying it arrives on the server; check journalctl -u rsyslog for TLS errors if it does not. The key is matching driver, CA, and certificate settings on both ends. Secure remote logging with rsyslog over TLS means set defaultnetstreamdriver to gtls, reference ca and cert files, and use omfwd with streamdrivermode to require tls for remote forwarding.. journalctl supports multiple output formats and choosing the right one depends on your goal. Use the default pager output for human reading and troubleshooting at the console; it formats messages in a readable timeline. For automation, -o json or -o json-pretty produce structured records you can pipe to jq or other parsers. -o verbose shows every available journal field and is useful for deep audits when you need metadata such as _EXE, _CMDLINE, _SYSTEMD_UNIT, and the exact monotonic timestamps. The -f option is indispensable for live monitoring because it follows new messages in real time. An example workflow: during an incident, tail with -f to watch incoming errors, then capture the same window with -o json for an external analyzer. A frequent misconception is that -o json lacks necessary metadata; in fact json and json-pretty include key fields, but verbose exposes the full record for forensic needs. Picking the right output reduces parsing errors and ensures you have the context required for post-incident reviews. Troubleshooting logging systems requires a structured approach because similar symptoms can have different causes. Start by checking service status with systemctl status rsyslog or systemctl status systemd-journald to see immediate failure messages. Check journalctl -u for unit-specific logs. Permissions issues are frequent: if rsyslog cannot write to a target file, verify ownership and mode. Disk space exhaustion is another common cause; use df -h and examine journald settings—SystemMaxUse and SystemKeepFree—to remedy runaway journal growth. Rule order errors appear when a broad selector earlier captures messages that specific rules should handle; use & stop to prevent duplicates and reorder files so specific rules load first. For remote logging, ensure firewalls allow the chosen ports (UDP/TCP 514 or TLS 6514) and that certificate paths and chains are correct; mismatched or unreadable cert files will block TLS. Finally, check for silent failures by tailing logs and using test messages with logger to trace delivery. The key idea is methodical checks: service health, file permissions, disk, rule logic, network, and certificates. This checklist reduces guesswork when logs stop being delivered or are missing. Let's summarize the essential concepts to remember. journald is the structured, binary journal of systemd and requires Storage=persistent to keep logs across reboots; pair that with SystemMaxUse and SystemKeepFree to avoid disk exhaustion. journalctl provides powerful filters—time ranges, priorities, and field selectors—and multiple output modes like JSON or verbose to suit scripting or auditing. rsyslog is the flexible forwarder that uses selectors and actions to route messages; rule order matters and & stop prevents duplication. Secure remote logging uses rsyslog TLS settings with the gtls driver and matching certificate configuration on client and server. Finally, troubleshooting follows a clear checklist: confirm service status, check permissions, verify disk space, test rule ordering, ensure network ports are open, and validate certificate chains. Keep these concepts in mind as a practical checklist when you build production-grade logging pipelines.

To close, remember three concise points: first, persist journald with Storage=persistent and enforce SystemMaxUse and SystemKeepFree to balance retention and disk safety. Second, master journalctl filtering and output modes so you can locate incidents and automate analysis with JSON. Third, design rsyslog rules carefully and use TLS for remote forwarding; rule order and & stop prevent duplication and TLS ensures confidentiality. These three actions—persistence, precise queries, and secure forwarding—form the spine of reliable logging.
